claim: RNA virus infections are detected by the RIG-I family of receptors.
source: RNA virus infections are detected by the RIG-I family of receptors, which induce type-I interferons through the mitochondrial protein MAVS.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about innate immune recognition of RNA viruses.

claim: RIG-I family receptors induce type-I interferons through the mitochondrial protein MAVS.
source: RNA virus infections are detected by the RIG-I family of receptors, which induce type-I interferons through the mitochondrial protein MAVS.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the RIG-I signaling pathway.

claim: MAVS forms large prion-like polymers that activate the cytosolic kinases IKK and TBK1.
source: MAVS forms large prion-like polymers that activate the cytosolic kinases IKK and TBK1, which in turn activate NF-κB and IRF3, respectively, to induce interferons.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript and confirmed by the current study.

claim: IKK and TBK1 activate NF-κB and IRF3, respectively, to induce interferons.
source: MAVS forms large prion-like polymers that activate the cytosolic kinases IKK and TBK1, which in turn activate NF-κB and IRF3, respectively, to induce interferons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the downstream signaling of these kinases.

claim: MAVS polymers recruit several TRAF proteins, including TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6, through distinct TRAF-binding motifs.
source: Here we show that MAVS polymers recruit several TRAF proteins, including TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6, through distinct TRAF-binding motifs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including co-immunoprecipitation and mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Mutations of TRAF-binding motifs that disrupted MAVS binding to TRAFs abrogated its ability to activate IRF3.
source: Mutations of these motifs that disrupted MAVS binding to TRAFs abrogated its ability to activate IRF3.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: IRF3 activation was abolished in cells lacking TRAF2, 5, and 6.
source: IRF3 activation was also abolished in cells lacking TRAF2, 5, and 6.
evidence: This is supported by experiments in triple knockout cells shown in Figure 2.

claim: TRAF proteins promoted ubiquitination reactions that recruited NEMO to the MAVS signaling complex.
source: These TRAF proteins promoted ubiquitination reactions that recruited NEMO to the MAVS signaling complex, leading to the activation of IKK and TBK1.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro reconstitution experiments and SILAC mass spectrometry data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: TRAF2, 5, and 6 play a crucial role in IRF3 activation in antiviral immune responses.
source: These results delineate the mechanism of MAVS signaling and reveal that TRAF2, 5, and 6, which are normally associated with NF-κB activation, also play a crucial role in IRF3 activation in antiviral immune responses.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: RLRs include RIG-I, MDA5, and LGP2.
source: RLRs include RIG-I, MDA5, and LGP2 (Yoneyama et al., 2004; Yoneyama and Fujita, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: All RLRs contain a DEAD/H-box RNA helicase domain, which binds to double-stranded RNA.
source: All RLRs contain a DEAD/H-box RNA helicase domain, which binds to double-stranded RNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RLR protein structure and function.

claim: RIG-I and MDA5, but not LGP2, harbor N-terminal tandem CARD domains that are crucial for triggering type-I IFN production.
source: RIG-I and MDA5, but not LGP2, harbor N-terminal tandem CARD domains that are crucial for triggering type-I IFN production.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RLR protein structure and function.

claim: RIG-I contains a C-terminal regulatory domain that specifically binds to RNA bearing 5′ triphosphate.
source: RIG-I also contains a C-terminal regulatory domain that specifically binds to RNA bearing 5′ triphosphate (Hornung et al., 2006; Pichlmair et al., 2006; Cui et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RIG-I and MDA5 activate MAVS, presumably through CARD–CARD interaction.
source: Upon binding to different viral RNA ligands, RIG-I and MDA5 activate another CARD-containing protein, mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS, also known as IPS-1, VISA, and CARDIF), presumably through CARD–CARD interaction.
evidence: This is established knowledge with some inference about the mechanism of interaction.

claim: MAVS activates the transcription factors IRF3 and NF-κB, leading to interferon induction.
source: MAVS in turn activates the transcription factors IRF3 and NF-κB, leading to interferon induction (Kawai et al., 2005; Meylan et al., 2005; Seth et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Sequential binding of RIG-I to viral RNAs and unanchored lysine-63 (K63) polyubiquitin chains promotes RIG-I to form higher order oligomers.
source: The sequential binding of RIG-I to viral RNAs and unanchored lysine-63 (K63) polyubiquitin chains promotes RIG-I to form higher order oligomers, which then rapidly induce MAVS polymerization.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: RIG-I oligomers rapidly induce MAVS polymerization.
source: The sequential binding of RIG-I to viral RNAs and unanchored lysine-63 (K63) polyubiquitin chains promotes RIG-I to form higher order oligomers, which then rapidly induce MAVS polymerization.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.

claim: MAVS polymers recruit other MAVS molecules on the mitochondrial surface to form larger polymers through a prion-like mechanism.
source: The MAVS polymers recruit other MAVS molecules on the mitochondrial surface to form larger polymers through a prion-like mechanism (Hou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research by the same group.

claim: Polyubiquitin binding to RIG-I is required for RIG-I activation.
source: Upstream of MAVS, polyubiquitin binding to RIG-I is required for RIG-I activation as described above.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.

claim: K63-linked polyubiquitin and the E2 UBC5 are required for IRF3 activation downstream of MAVS.
source: Downstream of MAVS, K63-linked polyubiquitin and the E2 UBC5 are required for IRF3 activation (Zeng et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research by the same group.

claim: NEMO functions as a ubiquitin sensor in different pathways that lead to NF-κB and IRF3 activation.
source: NEMO, the regulatory subunit of IKK and TBK1, functions as a ubiquitin sensor in different pathways that lead to NF-κB and IRF3 activation (Ea et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TANK, SINTBAD, NAP1, and STING have been found to associate with TBK1.
source: Additionally, several proteins, including TANK, SINTBAD, NAP1, and STING (also known as MITA, ERIS, and MPYS), have been found to associate with TBK1 (Sasai et al., 2006; Guo and Cheng, 2007; Ryzhakov and Randow, 2007; Ishikawa and Barber, 2008; Jin et al., 2008; Zhong et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Several E3 ligases including TRAF3, TRAF5, cIAP1/2, and MIB1/2 were proposed to regulate IRF3 activation downstream of MAVS.
source: Several E3 ligases including TRAF3, TRAF5, cIAP1/2, and MIB1/2 were proposed to regulate IRF3 activation downstream of MAVS (Saha et al., 2006; Mao et al., 2010; Tang and Wang, 2010; Li et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research by other groups.

claim: LUBAC has been shown to negatively regulate the RIG-I pathway.
source: In addition, LUBAC, an E3 ligase complex that synthesizes linear ubiquitin chains, has been shown to negatively regulate the RIG-I pathway (Inn et al., 2011; Belgnaoui et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research, though the current study challenges this conclusion.

claim: TRAF6 was identified as an IRF3 activator in the presence of activated MAVS.
source: To further dissect the mechanism of how MAVS propagates downstream signaling, we performed conventional purification and identified TRAF6 as an IRF3 activator in the presence of activated MAVS.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by biochemical purification and functional assays.

claim: TRAF2 and TRAF5 act redundantly with TRAF6 to activate both IRF3 and NF-κB in response to virus.
source: Moreover, by knocking down TRAF6 in Traf2/5-deficient cells, we found that TRAF2 and TRAF5 act redundantly with TRAF6 to activate both IRF3 and NF-κB in response to virus.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by genetic experiments in knockout cells.

claim: The E3 ligase activity of TRAF6 is essential in the TRAF6-dependent activation of IRF3 and NF-κB.
source: In addition, we provide evidence that the E3 ligase activity of TRAF6 is essential in the TRAF6-dependent activation of IRF3 and NF-κB, whereas the E3 ligase activity of TRAF2 is redundant with that of LUBAC in the Traf2-dependent pathway downstream of MAVS.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experiments with catalytically inactive mutants.

claim: The E3 ligase activity of TRAF2 is redundant with that of LUBAC in the Traf2-dependent pathway downstream of MAVS.
source: In addition, we provide evidence that the E3 ligase activity of TRAF6 is essential in the TRAF6-dependent activation of IRF3 and NF-κB, whereas the E3 ligase activity of TRAF2 is redundant with that of LUBAC in the Traf2-dependent pathway downstream of MAVS.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experiments with TRAF2 RING mutants and HOIP knockdown.

claim: Mutations of the binding sites for TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 on MAVS abolished the ability of MAVS to activate downstream signaling after virus infection.
source: Furthermore, mutations of the binding sites for TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 on MAVS abolished the ability of MAVS to activate downstream signaling after virus infection, without affecting its ability to form prion-like polymers.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutations of TRAF-binding sites on MAVS did not affect its ability to form prion-like polymers.
source: Furthermore, mutations of the binding sites for TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 on MAVS abolished the ability of MAVS to activate downstream signaling after virus infection, without affecting its ability to form prion-like polymers.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by SDD-AGE and sucrose gradient experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MAVS polymerization mutants failed to recruit TRAFs.
source: MAVS polymerization mutants, however, failed to recruit TRAFs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: NEMO formed a ubiquitination-dependent complex with TRAFs and MAVS, both in vitro and in cells.
source: Finally, we found that through its ubiquitin-binding domains, NEMO formed a ubiquitination-dependent complex with TRAFs and MAVS, both in vitro and in cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by in vitro reconstitution and SILAC experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: NEMO forms a complex with TRAFs and MAVS through its ubiquitin-binding domains.
source: Finally, we found that through its ubiquitin-binding domains, NEMO formed a ubiquitination-dependent complex with TRAFs and MAVS, both in vitro and in cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experiments with NEMO ubiquitin-binding domain mutants.

claim: IRF3 dimerization was detected when crude mitochondrial fraction from Sendai virus-infected cells was incubated with cytosolic extracts from uninfected cells.
source: When crude mitochondrial fraction (P5) from Sendai virus-infected HEK293T cells was incubated with cytosolic extracts (S5 or S100) from uninfected cells, along with [35S]-IRF3 and ATP, IRF3 dimerization was detected by native gel electrophoresis followed by autoradiography (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: IκBα phosphorylation was detected when crude mitochondrial fraction from Sendai virus-infected cells was incubated with cytosolic extracts from uninfected cells.
source: Similarly, IκBα phosphorylation was detected by immunoblotting with a phospho-IκBα specific antibody (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Purified MAVSΔTM expressed from E. coli forms functional polymers.
source: MAVSΔTM expressed and purified from E. coli forms functional polymers, thereby bypassing the requirement for its mitochondrial membrane localization (Hou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research by the same group.

claim: Both Q-A and Q-B fractions were required to support IRF3 activation in the in vitro assay.
source: In our previous study, HeLa S100 was separated by Q-Sepharose column into Q-A containing the flow-through and Q-B containing proteins eluted with 0.3 M NaCl (Zeng et al., 2009). Both Q-A and Q-B were required to support IRF3 activation in our in vitro assay.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research by the same group.

claim: The key factor in Q-A was identified as the ubiquitin E2 Ubc5.
source: The key factor in Q-A was identified as the ubiquitin E2 Ubc5 (Zeng et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research by the same group.

claim: IKKα/IKKβ double-deficient MEF cells activated IRF3 normally in response to infection by vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV).
source: Q-B contains multiple factors known to be important for virus-induced IRF3 activation, such as NEMO, TBK1, ubiquitin, and E1 (data not shown). Q-B also contains the IKK complex; however, IKKα/IKKβ double-deficient MEF cells activated IRF3 normally in response to infection by vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), an RNA virus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GST-NEMO without its N-terminal IKK-binding site (NEMOΔN) rescued IRF3 activity in Nemo−/− MEF cell extracts.
source: Moreover, GST-NEMO without its N-terminal IKK-binding site (NEMOΔN) rescued IRF3 activity in Nemo−/−(Ikbkg−/−) MEF cell extracts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating an IKK-independent role of NEMO in virus-induced IRF3 activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NEMO has an IKK-independent role in virus-induced IRF3 activation.
source: Moreover, GST-NEMO without its N-terminal IKK-binding site (NEMOΔN) rescued IRF3 activity in Nemo−/−(Ikbkg−/−) MEF cell extracts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating an IKK-independent role of NEMO in virus-induced IRF3 activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that NEMOΔN can rescue IRF3 activation.

claim: NEMOΔN pulled down endogenous TANK and TBK1 from Nemo−/− cell extracts.
source: NEMO has been reported to interact with TBK1 through TANK (Zhao et al., 2007). Indeed, NEMOΔN pulled down endogenous TANK and TBK1 from Nemo−/− cell extracts (NEMOΔN PD, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: After NEMO depletion, S100 lost its ability to support IRF3 dimerization in vitro.
source: After NEMO depletion by a NEMO antibody, S100 lost its ability to support IRF3 dimerization in vitro, and the activity was restored by adding back NEMO PD, but not NEMO alone (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: NEMO and the TBK1 complex function together in IRF3 activation.
source: This suggests that NEMO and the TBK1 complex function together in IRF3 activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that NEMO PD (containing TBK1 complex) is required for IRF3 activation.

claim: NEMOΔN PD does not fully replace Q-B in IRF3 activation in vitro even in the presence of ubiquitin and E1.
source: However, NEMOΔN PD does not fully replace Q-B in IRF3 activation in vitro even in the presence of ubiquitin and E1 (data not shown), indicating that additional factor(s) might be required for IRF3 activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (not shown) and leads to the inference that additional factors are required.

claim: TRAF6 supported IRF3 activation in a manner that depended on MAVSΔTM and the ubiquitin system.
source: To determine whether TRAF6 is important for IRF3 activation in vitro, we performed reconstitution experiments using purified proteins and found that TRAF6 supported IRF3 activation in a manner that depended on MAVSΔTM and the ubiquitin system (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: IRF3 activation by virus-activated mitochondria (P5) was dependent on TRAF6.
source: Similarly, IRF3 activation by virus-activated mitochondria (P5) was dependent on TRAF6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Cytosolic extracts from Traf6−/− primary MEF cells were severely defective in supporting IRF3 dimerization and IκBα phosphorylation in vitro.
source: Cytosolic extracts from Traf6−/− primary MEF cells were severely, albeit not completely, defective in supporting IRF3 dimerization and IκBα phosphorylation in vitro, and these defects were rescued by adding back wild-type TRAF6 (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: TRAF6 RING mutant (TRAF6-C70A) failed to rescue IRF3 activation in Traf6−/− cell extracts.
source: In contrast, TRAF6 RING mutant (TRAF6-C70A), TRAF6 Zinc finger deletion (TRAF6ΔZF), or TRAF6 with the TRAF-C domain replaced by a fragment of bacterial gyrase-B (T6RZC) (Wang et al., 2001) failed to rescue IRF3 activation in Traf6−/− cell extracts (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Both TRAF6 E3 ligase activity and its ability to interact with other proteins are important for IRF3 activation in vitro.
source: These results suggest that both TRAF6 E3 ligase activity and its ability to interact with other proteins, that is, MAVS (Seth et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2005), are important for IRF3 activation in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that both RING and TRAF-C domain mutants are defective.

claim: Traf6−/− cells exhibited normal virus-induced interferon production.
source: However, it has been shown that Traf6−/− cells exhibited normal virus-induced interferon production (Seth et al., 2005; Zeng et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.

claim: Traf6−/− primary MEF cells supported IRF3 and IKK activation in response to Sendai virus infection.
source: Consistent with these reports, Traf6−/− primary MEF cells supported IRF3 and IKK activation in response to Sendai virus infection, but were defective in activating IKK in response to IL-1β (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Traf6−/− primary MEF cells were defective in activating IKK in response to IL-1β.
source: Consistent with these reports, Traf6−/− primary MEF cells supported IRF3 and IKK activation in response to Sendai virus infection, but were defective in activating IKK in response to IL-1β (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Crude extracts (S5) from Traf2−/−/Traf5−/− (Traf2/5 DKO) MEF cells failed to support IRF3 dimerization or IκBα phosphorylation in vitro.
source: Indeed, crude extracts (S5) from Traf2−/−/Traf5−/− (Traf2/5 DKO) MEF cells failed to support IRF3 dimerization or IκBα phosphorylation in vitro; both activities were restored by adding back wild-type TRAF2 or TRAF5 (Figure 1G,H,I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G,H,I.

claim: TRAF2 RING deletion (TRAF2ΔR) did not impair IRF3 dimerization in cytosolic extracts (S5) from Traf2/5 DKO cells.
source: Unlike TRAF6, TRAF2 RING deletion (TRAF2ΔR) did not impair IRF3 dimerization in cytosolic extracts (S5) from Traf2/5 DKO cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Deletion of the TRAF-C domain from TRAF2 (TRAF2ΔC) abolished its activity.
source: In contrast, deletion of the TRAF-C domain from TRAF2 (TRAF2ΔC) abolished its activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: MEF cells lacking a single TRAF protein, TRAF2, TRAF3, or TRAF5, were largely normal in activating IRF3 in vitro.
source: MEF cells lacking a single TRAF protein, TRAF2, TRAF3, or TRAF5, were largely normal in activating IRF3 in vitro (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Traf2−/− MEFs induced IFNβ and IL6 normally in response to Sendai virus infection.
source: Similar to Traf6−/− MEFs, Traf2−/− MEFs induced IFNβ and IL6 normally in response to Sendai virus infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Traf2/5 DKO cells activated IRF3 and IKK and induced IFNβ normally after Sendai virus infection.
source: Moreover, in contrast to the profound defect of Traf2/5 DKO cell extracts in supporting IRF3 and IKK activation by MAVS, the DKO cells activated IRF3 and IKK and induced IFNβ normally after Sendai virus infection (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Knockdown of TRAF6 in Traf2/5 DKO cells abolished IRF3 and IKK activation and IFNβ induction by Sendai virus.
source: Importantly, knockdown of TRAF6 expression by short hairpin RNA (shTRAF6) in the DKO cells abolished IRF3 and IKK activation and IFNβ induction by Sendai virus, but did not impair STAT1 phosphorylation induced by IFNγ (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Knockdown of TRAF6 in Traf2/5 DKO cells did not impair STAT1 phosphorylation induced by IFNγ.
source: Importantly, knockdown of TRAF6 expression by short hairpin RNA (shTRAF6) in the DKO cells abolished IRF3 and IKK activation and IFNβ induction by Sendai virus, but did not impair STAT1 phosphorylation induced by IFNγ (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The defects in IRF3 and IκBα phosphorylation in the DKO+shTRAF6 cells were rescued by expressing RNAi-resistant WT TRAF6, but not the C70A mutant of TRAF6.
source: The defects in IRF3 and IκBα phosphorylation in the DKO+shTRAF6 cells were rescued by expressing RNAi-resistant WT TRAF6, but not the C70A mutant of TRAF6.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: VSV induction of IFNβ, IL6, IFNα, and CXCL10 was abolished in the DKO+shTRAF6 cells but rescued by WT TRAF6.
source: Similarly, VSV induction of several cytokines, including IFNβ, IL6, IFNα, and CXCL10, was abolished in the DKO+shTRAF6 cells but rescued by WT TRAF6 (Figure 2C–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: A TRAF6 mutant in which every lysine was substituted with an arginine (T6-K0) rescued the cytokine expression in the DKO+shTRAF6 cells.
source: A TRAF6 mutant in which every lysine was substituted with an arginine (T6-K0), but not TRAF6-C70A, rescued the cytokine expression in the DKO+shTRAF6 cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C–E.

claim: TRAF6 functions redundantly with TRAF2 and TRAF5 in a manner that depends on the E3 ligase activity of TRAF6 but not its ubiquitination at any lysine residue.
source: Thus, TRAF6 functions redundantly with TRAF2 and TRAF5 in a manner that depends on the E3 ligase activity of TRAF6 but not its ubiquitination at any lysine residue.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that T6-K0 rescues but C70A does not.

claim: Both WT and C34A mutant of TRAF2 rescued virus activation of IRF3 in DKO+shTRAF6 cells.
source: In contrast to a requirement of the E3 ligase activity of TRAF6 in MAVS signaling (Figure 2C–E), both WT and C34A mutant of TRAF2 rescued virus activation of IRF3 as well as the induction of IFNβ, IL6, IFNα, and CXCL10 in these cells (Figure 2F–H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E,F.

claim: WT and C34A TRAF2 rescued IκBα phosphorylation induced by TNFα, but not IL-1β, in DKO+shTRAF6 cells.
source: WT and C34A TRAF2 also rescued IκBα phosphorylation induced by TNFα, but not IL-1β, in DKO+shTRAF6 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: The E3 ligase activity of TRAF2 is either dispensable or redundant with that of another E3 ligase.
source: These results suggest that the E3 ligase activity of TRAF2 is either dispensable or redundant with that of another E3 ligase (see below).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that TRAF2 C34A mutant can rescue signaling.

claim: The knockdown of MAVS blocked IRF3 activation and IFNβ induction by VSV.
source: As expected, the knockdown of MAVS blocked IRF3 activation and IFNβ induction by VSV.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The knockdown of HOIL-1 slightly enhanced IRF3 activation and IFNβ induction as compared to the control cells.
source: The knockdown of HOIL-1 slightly enhanced IRF3 activation and IFNβ induction as compared to the control cells, consistent with its role as a negative regulator of RIG-I signaling (Inn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B and is consistent with prior research.

claim: The knockdown of HOIP, Sharpin, or TRAF3 did not appreciably affect IRF3 activation and modestly inhibited IFNβ induction by VSV.
source: However, the knockdown of HOIP, Sharpin, or TRAF3 did not appreciably affect IRF3 activation and modestly inhibited IFNβ induction by VSV (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Loss of Sharpin slightly reduced IFNβ induction by VSV.
source: A previous report showed that IFNβ induction is enhanced in MEF cells derived from the mouse strain Sharpincpdm, which is deficient in Sharpin expression (Belgnaoui et al., 2012). Contrary to this report, we found that loss of Sharpin slightly reduced IFNβ induction by VSV (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and contradicts prior research.

claim: Re-introducing Sharpin back into Sharpin-deficient MEFs did not inhibit or enhance the activation of IRF3 or IKK by Sendai virus.
source: Re-introducing Sharpin back into Sharpin-deficient MEFs did not inhibit or enhance the activation of IRF3 or IKK by Sendai virus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Tetracycline-inducible knockdown of HOIP in U2OS cells modestly inhibited the activation of IRF3 and induction of IFNβ by VSV.
source: Consistent with our model that LUBAC is not a negative regulator of MAVS signaling, tetracycline-inducible knockdown of HOIP in the human osteosarcoma cell line U2OS modestly inhibited the activation of IRF3 and induction of IFNβ by VSV (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The depletion of HOIP abolished IRF3 activation by VSV in cells expressing TRAF2-ΔRING, but not in those expressing WT TRAF2 or TRAF6.
source: Interestingly, the depletion of HOIP abolished IRF3 activation by VSV in the cells expressing TRAF2-ΔRING, but not in those expressing WT TRAF2 or TRAF6.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The defect of IRF3 activation in the HOIP-depleted cells that expressed TRAF2-ΔRING was rescued by WT HOIP but not the catalytically inactive HOIP mutant, C693S/C696S.
source: The defect of IRF3 activation in the HOIP-depleted cells that expressed TRAF2-ΔRING was rescued by WT HOIP but not the catalytically inactive HOIP mutant, C693S/C696S (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Knockdown of Sharpin, and to a lesser extent HOIL-1, inhibited IRF3 and IKK activation in the Traf2/Traf5 DKO + shTRAF6 cells expressing TRAF2 ΔRING.
source: Similar to HOIP, knockdown of Sharpin, and to a lesser extent HOIL-1, inhibited IRF3 and IKK activation in the Traf2/Traf5 DKO + shTRAF6 cells expressing TRAF2 ΔRING (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The E3 ligase activity of LUBAC can support MAVS signaling when the functions of the TRAF proteins are compromised.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the E3 ligase activity of LUBAC can support MAVS signaling when the functions of the TRAF proteins are compromised.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that HOIP is required when TRAF2 RING is deleted.

claim: MAVS harbors binding motifs for TRAF2, TRAF3, TRAF5, and TRAF6.
source: MAVS harbors binding motifs for TRAF2, TRAF3, TRAF5, and TRAF6 (Seth et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2005; Saha et al., 2006; Paz et al., 2011) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research and is illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: The motif PVQET (143–147) is known to bind TRAF2 and TRAF5, and perhaps TRAF3.
source: The motif PVQET (143–147) is known to bind TRAF2 and TRAF5, and perhaps TRAF3, whereas two motifs, PGENSE (153–158) and PEENEY (455–460) bind TRAF6.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.

claim: Two motifs, PGENSE (153–158) and PEENEY (455–460) bind TRAF6.
source: The motif PVQET (143–147) is known to bind TRAF2 and TRAF5, and perhaps TRAF3, whereas two motifs, PGENSE (153–158) and PEENEY (455–460) bind TRAF6.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.

claim: The second TRAF6-binding motif has been suggested to bind TRAF3.
source: The second TRAF6-binding motif has also been suggested to bind TRAF3 (Paz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.

claim: TRAF6 and TRAF2 shifted to high-molecular weight fractions together with MAVS polymers in response to Sendai virus infection.
source: We showed previously that TRAF6 and TRAF2 shifted to high-molecular weight fractions together with MAVS polymers in response to Sendai virus infection (Hou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research by the same group.

claim: Mutations of the TRAF2/3/5 (Q145N) or TRAF6 [E155D/E457D (2ED)] binding sites did not affect IRF3 activation by Sendai virus.
source: Mutations of the TRAF2/3/5 (Q145N) or TRAF6 [E155D/E457D (2ED)] binding sites did not affect IRF3 activation by Sendai virus (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mutations of all known TRAF-binding sites (QN2ED) abolished IRF3 activation.
source: In contrast, mutations of all known TRAF-binding sites (QN2ED) abolished IRF3 activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: QN2ED, but not Q145N or 2ED, mutations in MAVS abolished IFNβ and IL-6 induction by Sendai virus.
source: Similarly, QN2ED, but not Q145N or 2ED, mutations in MAVS abolished IFNβ and IL-6 induction by Sendai virus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: QN2ED MAVS permitted higher levels of VSV replication.
source: QN2ED MAVS also permitted higher levels of VSV replication (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The TRAF6 complex from virus-infected cells contained WT and Q145N MAVS, but not 2ED or QN2ED MAVS.
source: Immunoprecipitation with Flag antibody revealed that the TRAF6 complex from the virus-infected cells contained WT and Q145N MAVS, but not 2ED or QN2ED MAVS (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The TRAF2 complex contained WT and 2ED MAVS, but not Q145N or QN2ED MAVS.
source: In contrast, the TRAF2 complex contained WT and 2ED MAVS, but not Q145N or QN2ED MAVS (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The QN2ED mutant formed high molecular weight aggregates after virus infection.
source: Like WT MAVS, the QN2ED mutant formed high molecular weight aggregates after virus infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that its inability to activate IRF3 is likely due to defective recruitment of TRAF proteins rather than a defect in polymerization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The inability of QN2ED MAVS to activate IRF3 is likely due to defective recruitment of TRAF proteins rather than a defect in polymerization.
source: Like WT MAVS, the QN2ED mutant formed high molecular weight aggregates after virus infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that its inability to activate IRF3 is likely due to defective recruitment of TRAF proteins rather than a defect in polymerization.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that QN2ED can polymerize but cannot activate IRF3.

claim: In Traf6−/− cells, Q145N but not 2ED MAVS was completely defective in inducing IFNβ.
source: In Traf6−/− cells, Q145N but not 2ED MAVS was completely defective in inducing IFNβ, but this defect was rescued by ectopic expression of WT but not C70A TRAF6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: A functional TRAF6 is indispensable for signaling through the two TRAF6-binding sites.
source: These results indicate that a functional TRAF6 was indispensable for signaling through the two TRAF6-binding sites (i.e., no other TRAF proteins, such as TRAF3, could substitute the function of TRAF6).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that Q145N MAVS cannot signal in Traf6−/− cells.

claim: In Traf2/5 DKO cells, 2ED but not Q145N MAVS was defective in inducing IFNβ.
source: In Traf2/5 DKO cells, 2ED but not Q145N MAVS was defective in inducing IFNβ, but this defect was rescued by WT TRAF2 and partially rescued by the C34A and RING-deleted mutant of TRAF2 (TRAF2ΔRING) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: In Traf2−/− or Traf5−/− cells, only QN2ED MAVS failed to rescue IFNβ induction.
source: In Traf2−/− or Traf5−/− cells, only QN2ED MAVS failed to rescue IFNβ induction, suggesting that TRAF2 and TRAF5 could functionally substitute each other (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: TRAF2 and TRAF5 can functionally substitute each other.
source: In Traf2−/− or Traf5−/− cells, only QN2ED MAVS failed to rescue IFNβ induction, suggesting that TRAF2 and TRAF5 could functionally substitute each other (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that single knockouts can be rescued by MAVS with only one TRAF2/5 binding site intact.

claim: Traf3−/− cells could support IRF3 activation by WT, Q145N, and 2ED MAVS, but not QN2ED MAVS.
source: Similar to WT cells (Figure 4B), Traf3−/− cells could support IRF3 activation by WT, Q145N, and 2ED MAVS, but not QN2ED MAVS (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Traf6−/− cells could not support IRF3 activation by Q145N MAVS.
source: In contrast, Traf6−/− cells could not support IRF3 activation by Q145N MAVS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: MAVS signals through its specific TRAF-binding motifs that recruit TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6, which then function in parallel to activate IRF3 and NF-κB.
source: Taken together (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), these results strongly support the conclusion that MAVS signals through its specific TRAF-binding motifs that recruit TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6, which then function in parallel to activate IRF3 and NF-κB.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Each of the point mutations E26A, R64A, and R65A in MAVS CARD abrogated the ability of MAVS to induce an IFNβ luciferase reporter gene.
source: Each of these mutations abrogated the ability of MAVS to induce an IFNβ luciferase (IFNβ-Luc) reporter gene stably integrated in HEK293T cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: MAVS containing point mutations in the CARD domain failed to activate IRF3 or form aggregates following viral infection.
source: Unlike wild-type MAVS, which activated IRF3 and formed SDS-resistant aggregates following viral infection, MAVS containing point mutations in the CARD domain failed to activate IRF3 or form aggregates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Only WT MAVS activated IRF3 after Sendai virus infection and formed high molecular weight particles that sedimented to the bottom layers after sucrose gradient ultracentrifugation.
source: Similarly, in HEK293T cells in which endogenous MAVS was knocked down by shRNA and replaced by RNAi-resistant MAVS WT or CARD mutants, only WT MAVS activated IRF3 after Sendai virus infection and formed high molecular weight particles that sedimented to the bottom layers after sucrose gradient ultracentrifugation (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Each of the point mutations in MAVS CARD abolished the virus-induced interaction between TRAF6 and MAVS.
source: Importantly, each of the point mutations in MAVS CARD abolished the virus-induced interaction between TRAF6 and MAVS (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The mutations that disrupt MAVS polymerization abrogated its binding to TRAF2 and TRAF5.
source: The mutations that disrupt MAVS polymerization also abrogated its binding to TRAF2 and TRAF5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: MAVS polymerization is important for the recruitment of TRAF6, TRAF2, TRAF5, and likely other signaling molecules.
source: These results strongly suggest that MAVS polymerization is important for the recruitment of TRAF6, TRAF2, TRAF5, and likely other signaling molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that polymerization mutants cannot recruit TRAFs.

claim: K63 polyubiquitination is important for IRF3 and IKK activation by MAVS in vitro.
source: The strongest defect in IRF3 dimerization and IκBα phosphorylation was observed in cell extracts containing K63R, suggesting that K63 polyubiquitination is important for IRF3 and IKK activation by MAVS in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MAVS and TRAF2 co-immunoprecipitated with Flag-NEMO after incubation at 30°C but not at 0°C.
source: MAVS and TRAF2 were found to co-immunoprecipitate (Co-IP) with Flag-NEMO after incubation at 30°C but not at 0°C (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The MAVS-TRAF2-NEMO interaction was blocked when a deubiquitination enzyme was included in the reaction mixture.
source: The MAVS-TRAF2-NEMO interaction was blocked when a deubiquitination enzyme, which contains the ovarian tumor type (OTU) domain of the Crimean Congo hemorrahagic fever virus, was included in the reaction mixture.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A NEMO mutant (UBDm; Y308S/H413A/C417A) failed to pull down the TRAF2-MAVS complex.
source: Moreover, a NEMO mutant (UBDm; Y308S/H413A/C417A), which contained point mutations in both ubiquitin-binding domains, failed to pull down the TRAF2-MAVS complex (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: MAVS and TRAF2 form a MAVS-induced ubiquitination-dependent signaling complex with NEMO in vitro.
source: These results suggest that MAVS and TRAF2 form a MAVS-induced ubiquitination-dependent signaling complex with NEMO in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that the interaction depends on ubiquitination and NEMO ubiquitin-binding domains.

claim: PLK1, TRAF2, and cIAP1 bound to NEMO in a manner that depended on MAVS and UBD of NEMO.
source: Among the proteins enriched in the heavy samples, we found that PLK1, TRAF2, and cIAP1 bound to NEMO in a manner that depended on MAVS and UBD of NEMO (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by SILAC mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All three subunits of the LUBAC complex, HOIP, HOIL-1, and Sharpin, bound to NEMO in a UBD-dependent manner.
source: All three subunits of the LUBAC complex, HOIP, HOIL-1, and Sharpin, bound to NEMO in a UBD-dependent manner, but this binding was largely independent of stimulation by MAVS.
evidence: This is supported by SILAC mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LUBAC binding to NEMO was largely independent of stimulation by MAVS.
source: All three subunits of the LUBAC complex, HOIP, HOIL-1, and Sharpin, bound to NEMO in a UBD-dependent manner, but this binding was largely independent of stimulation by MAVS.
evidence: This is supported by SILAC mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TRAF6, TRAF3, TRAF2, A20, and MAVS associated with NEMO WT, but not NEMO UBDm, after VSV infection.
source: Among the proteins that associated with NEMO WT, but not NEMO UBDm, after VSV infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), several were known NEMO-interacting proteins, including TRAF6, TRAF3, TRAF2, A20, and MAVS.
evidence: This is supported by SILAC mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MAVS and TRAF2 were the only common proteins identified by the in vitro and cell-based SILAC experiments.
source: A comparison of the NEMO interacting proteins identified by the in vitro and cell-based SILAC experiments revealed only two common proteins, MAVS and TRAF2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by SILAC mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Five ubiquitination sites on TRAF2 were detected by mass spectrometry, including K31, K148, K195, K313, and K481.
source: Five ubiquitination sites on TRAF2 were detected by mass spectrometry, including K31, K148, K195, K313, and K481 as illustrated in Figure 6D.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: K31 was identified as an autoubiquitination site of TRAF2 in the TNF pathway.
source: Among these lysines, K31 was identified as an autoubiquitination site of TRAF2 in the TNF pathway (Li et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.

claim: Both WT and 5KR TRAF2 rescued the induction of IFNβ, IL6, and CXCL10 by VSV.
source: Both WT and 5KR TRAF2 rescued the induction of IFNβ, IL6, and CXCL10 by VSV (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E–G.

claim: Knockdown of HOIP abolished the expression of cytokines in cells expressing TRAF2-5KR, but not wild type TRAF2.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of HOIP abolished the expression of these cytokines in cells expressing TRAF2-5KR, but not wild type TRAF2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E–G.

claim: Ubiquitinated TRAF2 may function redundantly with another ubiquitination target of HOIP.
source: These results, together with the results shown in Figure 3, suggest that ubiquitinated TRAF2 may function redundantly with another ubiquitination target of HOIP.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that HOIP is required when TRAF2 ubiquitination sites are mutated.

claim: NEMO has been reported to be ubiquitinated at lysine 285 and 309.
source: NEMO has been reported to be ubiquitinated at lysine 285 and 309, and this modification is important for NF-κB activation (Abbott et al., 2004; Tokunaga et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.

claim: Nemo−/− MEF cells stably expressing NEMO K285/309R mutant produced IFNβ and IL6 after VSV infection at levels similar to cells expressing wild-type NEMO.
source: We found that Nemo−/− MEF cells stably expressing NEMO K285/309R mutant produced IFNβ and IL6 after VSV infection and that the cytokine levels were similar to those produced by cells expressing wild-type NEMO (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A–C.

claim: Cells expressing NEMO-UBDm failed to induce cytokines after VSV infection.
source: In contrast, the cells expressing NEMO-UBDm failed to induce the cytokines after VSV infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A–C.

claim: Signal-dependent ubiquitination of NEMO was detected at K285, K325, K342, and K344 by mass spectrometry.
source: NEMO was purified under denaturing conditions and analyzed by nanoLC-MS/MS (see 'Materials and methods'), which detected signal-dependent ubiquitination of NEMO at K285, K325, K342, and K344 (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Nemo−/− MEF cells stably expressing NEMO 6KR mutant supported virus-induced cytokine production similar to those expressing wild-type NEMO.
source: However, Nemo−/− MEF cells stably expressing NEMO 6KR (K111/285/309/325/342/344R) mutant still supported virus-induced cytokine production similar to those expressing wild-type NEMO (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E,F.

claim: NEMO 13KR mutant could support IRF3 dimerization in Nemo-deficient cell extracts in the presence of MAVSΔTM.
source: We also constructed a NEMO mutant in which 13 conserved lysine residues were substituted with arginine (13KR) and found that this mutant could still support IRF3 dimerization in Nemo-deficient cell extracts in the presence of MAVSΔTM (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G,H.

claim: NEMO ubiquitination per se is dispensable for IRF3 activation in the MAVS pathway.
source: These results suggest that NEMO ubiquitination per se is dispensable for IRF3 activation in the MAVS pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that NEMO mutants lacking ubiquitination sites can still support IRF3 activation.

claim: Ubiquitination of multiple targets as well as unanchored K63 polyubiquitin chains function cooperatively to recruit NEMO and other signaling molecules to the MAVS polymers and promote the activation of IKK and TBK1.
source: It is likely that ubiquitination of multiple targets as well as unanchored K63 polyubiquitin chains function cooperatively to recruit NEMO and other signaling molecules to the MAVS polymers and promote the activation of IKK and TBK1 (Figure 8 and 'Discussion').
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: Cells lacking an individual TRAF protein, including TRAF2, TRAF3, TRAF5, and TRAF6, could still induce IFNβ normally in response to virus infection.
source: Although it is known that MAVS contains binding sites for several TRAF proteins (Seth et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2005), the role of these TRAF proteins in MAVS signaling has been enigmatic because cells lacking an individual TRAF protein, including TRAF2, TRAF3, TRAF5, and TRAF6, could still induce IFNβ normally in response to virus infection (Seth et al., 2005; Konno et al., 2009; Zeng et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.

claim: Compound deletion of TRAF6, TRAF2, and TRAF5 completely abolished IFNβ induction by Sendai virus and VSV.
source: In this report, we demonstrated that compound deletion of TRAF6, TRAF2, and TRAF5 completely abolished IFNβ induction by Sendai virus and VSV, suggesting that these proteins function redundantly in vivo to activate the downstream signaling cascades after they are recruited to the cognate binding sites on MAVS.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 function redundantly in vivo to activate the downstream signaling cascades after they are recruited to the cognate binding sites on MAVS.
source: In this report, we demonstrated that compound deletion of TRAF6, TRAF2, and TRAF5 completely abolished IFNβ induction by Sendai virus and VSV, suggesting that these proteins function redundantly in vivo to activate the downstream signaling cascades after they are recruited to the cognate binding sites on MAVS.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that triple knockout abolishes signaling.

claim: The redundant function of the TRAF proteins was not recapitulated in the cell free assay.
source: Such redundant function of the TRAF proteins was not recapitulated in our cell free assay, in which IRF3 activation by MAVS was strongly inhibited in Traf6-deficient extracts, and largely abolished in the absence of TRAF2 and TRAF5.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing in vitro and cell-based assays.

claim: TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 mediate the activation of IKK and NF-κB.
source: Currently, the prevailing view is that TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 mediate the activation of IKK and NF-κB, whereas TRAF3 is important for the activation of TBK1 and IRF3.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the prevailing view in the field.

claim: TRAF3 is important for the activation of TBK1 and IRF3.
source: Currently, the prevailing view is that TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 mediate the activation of IKK and NF-κB, whereas TRAF3 is important for the activation of TBK1 and IRF3.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the prevailing view in the field, which the current study challenges.

claim: TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 are essential for the activation of both IKK and TBK1 by MAVS.
source: However, here we showed that TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 are essential for the activation of both IKK and TBK1 by MAVS, whereas TRAF3 is dispensable.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study that challenges the prevailing view.

claim: TRAF3 is dispensable for MAVS signaling.
source: However, here we showed that TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 are essential for the activation of both IKK and TBK1 by MAVS, whereas TRAF3 is dispensable.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The TRAF6-binding site (455-PEENEY-460) of MAVS also binds to TRAF3.
source: Paz et al. have recently shown that the TRAF6-binding site (455-PEENEY-460) of MAVS also binds to TRAF3 and that this binding is important for MAVS signaling (Paz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.

claim: In cells expressing a MAVS mutant lacking the TRAF2/5 binding sites (Q145N), activation of IRF3 and production of IFNβ were completely abolished in cells depleted of TRAF6.
source: Our data showed that in cells expressing a MAVS mutant lacking the TRAF2/5 binding sites (Q145N), activation of IRF3 and production of IFNβ were completely abolished in cells depleted of TRAF6, indicating that other TRAF proteins, including TRAF3, could not substitute the function of TRAF6.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Other TRAF proteins, including TRAF3, could not substitute the function of TRAF6.
source: Our data showed that in cells expressing a MAVS mutant lacking the TRAF2/5 binding sites (Q145N), activation of IRF3 and production of IFNβ were completely abolished in cells depleted of TRAF6, indicating that other TRAF proteins, including TRAF3, could not substitute the function of TRAF6.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that Q145N MAVS cannot signal in Traf6−/− cells.

claim: IRF3 activation requires certain adaptor proteins such as MAVS, STING, and TRIF.
source: A possible explanation for these observations is that IRF3 activation requires certain adaptor proteins such as MAVS, STING, and TRIF.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: STING simultaneously binds to TBK1 and IRF3, thereby specifying IRF3 phosphorylation by TBK1.
source: Indeed, we have recently shown that STING simultaneously binds to TBK1 and IRF3, thereby specifying IRF3 phosphorylation by TBK1 (Tanaka and Chen, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research by the same group.

claim: Several innate immunity pathways, such as the TLR and IL-1 pathways, could lead to activation of TBK1 but not IRF3.
source: This mechanism explains why several innate immunity pathways, such as the TLR and IL-1 pathways, could lead to activation of TBK1 but not IRF3 (Clark et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.

claim: Each TRAF binding motif of MAVS has a low affinity for the TRAF proteins.
source: Presumably, each TRAF binding motif of MAVS has a low affinity for the TRAF proteins, but the polymerization of MAVS significantly increases the avidity of the interaction, resulting in the recruitment of the TRAF proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: The polymerization of MAVS significantly increases the avidity of the interaction with TRAF proteins, resulting in the recruitment of the TRAF proteins.
source: Presumably, each TRAF binding motif of MAVS has a low affinity for the TRAF proteins, but the polymerization of MAVS significantly increases the avidity of the interaction, resulting in the recruitment of the TRAF proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: The recruitment of TRAFs to the MAVS polymers may lead to the oligomerization of TRAFs, which activates their ubiquitin E3 ligase activity.
source: The recruitment of TRAFs to the MAVS polymers may lead to the oligomerization of TRAFs, which activates their ubiquitin E3 ligase activity (Wang et al., 2001; Sun et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors based on prior research.

claim: The E3 ligase activity of TRAF6 is important for IRF3 activation because mutation of the RING domain in TRAF6 abolishes its activity.
source: The E3 ligase activity of TRAF6 is likely important for IRF3 activation because mutation of the RING domain in TRAF6 abolishes its activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that TRAF6 RING mutants cannot rescue IRF3 activation.

claim: The RING domain of TRAF2 is important for IRF3 activation only when the catalytic activity of HOIP is abrogated.
source: Interestingly, the RING domain of TRAF2 is important for IRF3 activation only when the catalytic activity of HOIP is abrogated, suggesting that TRAF2 and HOIP may have redundant functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that TRAF2 RING mutant requires HOIP.

claim: TRAF2 and HOIP may have redundant functions.
source: Interestingly, the RING domain of TRAF2 is important for IRF3 activation only when the catalytic activity of HOIP is abrogated, suggesting that TRAF2 and HOIP may have redundant functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that TRAF2 RING mutant requires HOIP.

claim: HOIP is dispensable for IRF3 activation in cells expressing TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6.
source: HOIP is dispensable for IRF3 activation in cells expressing TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The loss of TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 completely abolishes IRF3 activation in cells expressing other E3s such as LUBAC, cIAPs, and TRAF3.
source: Conversely, the loss of TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 completely abolishes IRF3 activation in cells expressing other E3s such as LUBAC, cIAPs, and TRAF3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 are the major E3s that mediate the activation of IKK and TBK1 downstream of MAVS.
source: These results indicate that TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 are the major E3s that mediate the activation of IKK and TBK1 downstream of MAVS.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Both IKK and TBK1 employ NEMO as an essential regulatory subunit for their activation.
source: How do TRAF2, TRAF5, and TRAF6 activate IKK and TBK1? Both IKK and TBK1 employ NEMO as an essential regulatory subunit for their activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of NEMO in kinase activation.

claim: NEMO contains two ubiquitin-binding domains, which are essential for the activation of IKK and TBK1 in response to virus infection.
source: NEMO contains two ubiquitin-binding domains, which are essential for the activation of IKK and TBK1 in response to virus infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mutations of NEMO lysines to arginine did not impair the ability of NEMO to support IRF3 activation by MAVS.
source: Although we could detect ubiquitination of NEMO at multiple lysines, mutations of these lysines to arginine did not impair the ability of NEMO to support IRF3 activation by MAVS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: HOIP may have an additional ubiquitination target that functions redundantly with TRAF2 ubiquitination to mediate IRF3 activation.
source: Thus, HOIP may have an additional ubiquitination target that functions redundantly with TRAF2 ubiquitination to mediate IRF3 activation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: Multiple ubiquitin E3s are recruited to MAVS, and each E3 targets ubiquitination of distinct proteins, which function cooperatively and redundantly to activate IKK and TBK1.
source: An emerging theme from this work is that multiple ubiquitin E3s are recruited to MAVS, and each E3 targets ubiquitination of distinct proteins, which function cooperatively and redundantly to activate IKK and TBK1.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Sumoylation of a group of DNA repair proteins is responsible for the repair of DNA double-strand breaks.
source: A similar model has recently been proposed for the regulation of DNA repair by sumoylation (Psakhye and Jentsch, 2012). It was shown that sumoylation of a group of DNA repair proteins ('protein group'), rather than a specific protein target, is responsible for the repair of DNA double-strand breaks.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research used as an analogy.
